chunks: From him, from Ibn Mahbub, from Salih ibn Razin, from Ibn Ashyam, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him).

Regarding a slave who was permitted by his masters to trade, a man gave him one thousand dirhams and said to him: 'Buy a person with it, free him on my behalf, and perform Hajj with the remainder.' Then the owner of the thousand died. The slave went and bought his father, freed him on behalf of the deceased, and gave him the remainder to perform Hajj on behalf of the deceased, so he performed Hajj for him. This reached the masters of his father, his masters, and all the heirs of the deceased, and they all disputed over the thousand. The masters of the manumitter said: 'You bought your father with our money.' The heirs said: 'You bought your father with our money.' The masters of the slave said: 'You bought your father with our money.'

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'As for the Hajj, it has passed with what is in it and is not returned. As for the manumitted one, he is returned to slavery for the masters of his father. And whichever of the two parties establishes proof that he bought his father from their money, he has slavery over him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a slave using entrusted funds to buy and free his father, and who owns him?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) resolves the dispute by affirming the validity of the Hajj performed with the remainder, while ruling that the freed father's manumission is conditional upon proof of which party's funds were used for his purchase. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of 'return to slavery' (rad fi al-riq) when the source of emancipation funds is contested, ensuring that the rightful owner retains their claim. The case underscores the importance of evidentiary burden in commercial entrustments (amanah) within the context of family and inheritance law.
